subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: Find the condition that the tangents drawn from the exterior point (0,0) to S ≡ x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 are perpendicular to each other.

mark_split.label: Angle between the pair of tangents
Substitute r and S₁₁ and simplify

insider_note: The formula is written with HALF the angle, so perpendicular tangents mean θ/2 = 45° and tan 45° = 1 — students who put θ = 90° straight into tan θ get an undefined value and stop.

steps.label: Angle between the pair of tangents
steps.margin_note: One mark. Note that the formula uses θ/2, not θ. The line of symmetry through the centre halves the angle.
steps.memory_tip: tan(θ/2) = r/√S₁₁ — radius over the length of the tangent.
lines: Let θ be the angle between the pair of
tangents drawn from P(0, 0) to S = 0.
steps.why: The line joining the external point to the centre bisects the angle between the two tangents, so each half-angle sits in a right-angled triangle whose opposite side is r and whose adjacent side is the tangent length √S₁₁.
common_mistakes: Writing tan θ = r/√S₁₁ and losing the half.
Using the radius as the adjacent side and the tangent length as the opposite.

steps.label: Put the angle equal to 90°
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Perpendicular means θ = 90°, so θ/2 = 45° and tan 45° = 1.
steps.memory_tip: Perpendicular tangents: θ = 90°, half of it is 45°, and tan 45° = 1.
steps.why: Setting the half-angle to 45° makes the tangent of it exactly 1, so the radius equals the tangent length. Squaring both sides removes the root and gives a condition on the coefficients.
common_mistakes: Substituting θ = 90° into tan θ, which is not defined.

steps.label: Substitute r and S₁₁ and simplify
steps.margin_note: The last two marks. With the point (0, 0), S₁₁ collapses to c alone.
steps.memory_tip: At the origin every term of S₁₁ except c is zero, so S₁₁ = c.
steps.why: Substituting the origin into S kills every term that carries an x or a y, so S₁₁ is just c. Setting r² = S₁₁ then gives g² + f² − c = c, and moving c across gives the condition.
common_mistakes: Writing S₁₁ = 0 because the point is the origin.
Stopping at g² + f² − c = c without collecting the c terms.

steps.label: The picture
steps.margin_note: No mark of its own; the question does not ask for a diagram. It is the only way to see where the half-angle comes from.
steps.memory_tip: The line from the outside point to the centre splits the angle into two equal halves.

elements.text: the line to C halves the angle θ

steps.why: The two tangents from O are equal in length and the figure is symmetric about the line OC, so OC bisects the angle between them. That gives a right-angled triangle with the radius opposite the half-angle and the tangent length adjacent to it, which is exactly tan(θ/2) = r/√S₁₁.
common_mistakes: Marking the full angle θ inside the right-angled triangle.
Drawing the radius to a point that is not where the tangent touches.
